guide.title: Inference for quantitative data: review guide
guide.intro: This unit uses sample means and t procedures to estimate and test claims about population means, including paired and two-sample comparisons.

sections.title: Sampling distributions of a mean
body: The sample mean x̄ has mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n. By the central limit theorem, its distribution is approximately normal when n is large (often n ≥ 30), even if the population is skewed.
points: If the population is normal, x̄ is normal for any n.

sections.title: t intervals
body: When σ is unknown, use s and a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. Conditions: random sample, 10% condition, and a normal population or large n (check a graph for strong skew or outliers when n is small).
points: Paired data (the same subjects twice, or matched pairs): analyse the differences with one-sample t procedures.
Two independent groups: use two-sample t procedures. If the interval for μ₁ − μ₂ excludes 0, there is convincing evidence of a difference.

sections.title: t tests
body: Test statistic = (statistic − null value)/standard error. Find the p-value from the t distribution and compare with α. State the conclusion in context.
points: Choose paired versus two-sample by how the data were collected, not by the numbers.

example.prompt: A random sample of 16 bags has mean weight 498 g and s = 8 g. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight (t* = 2.131 for df = 15).

misconceptions: It is the distribution of x̄ that becomes approximately normal, not the data.
With σ unknown, use t*. It approaches z* as n grows.
Measurements on the same subjects are paired. Analyse the differences.

questions.prompt: A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. For random samples of size 25, what are the mean and standard deviation of x̄?
choiceExplanations: 10 is the population standard deviation. Sample means vary less, by a factor of √n.
This swaps the mean and the standard deviation.
0.4 divides σ by n instead of by √n.

questions.prompt: A population is strongly skewed to the right. Random samples of size 40 are taken. What is the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄?
choices: Strongly skewed to the right, like the population
questions.explanation: By the central limit theorem, with n = 40 the distribution of sample means is approximately normal even though the population is skewed.
choiceExplanations: It is approximately normal, not exactly, because the population is not normal.
Nothing suggests a uniform shape. Sample means pile up near μ.
Individual values are skewed, but averages of 40 values are much less so.

questions.prompt: A student wants to estimate the mean nightly sleep of all students at a school from a random sample of 30 students. σ is unknown. Which procedure fits?
choices: Two-sample t-interval for a difference of means
questions.explanation: One quantitative variable, one group, an estimate, and σ unknown: a one-sample t-interval.
choiceExplanations: There is only one group, so there is no difference to estimate.
Chi-square tests are for categorical variables, and this asks for an estimate, not a test.
Sleep time is quantitative, so this is about a mean, not a proportion.

questions.prompt: A random sample of 25 values has x̄ = 20 and s = 5. Using t* = 2.064 (df = 24), what is the 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.explanation: SE = 5/√25 = 1. Margin = 2.064 × 1 = 2.064, so the interval is 20 ± 2.064.
choiceExplanations: This uses s = 5 as the standard error instead of s/√n = 1.
This divides s by n (5/25 = 0.2) instead of by √n.
This uses z* = 1.96. With σ unknown, use t* = 2.064.

questions.prompt: Fifteen students take a test, attend a review session, and take a similar test again. Which procedure tests whether the session raised scores?
choices: A paired t-test on the differences
questions.explanation: Each student gives two linked scores, so the data are paired. Test the mean of the differences.
choiceExplanations: A two-sample t-test needs two independent groups. These are the same students measured twice.
Scores are quantitative. Chi-square tests are for categorical data.
The question is about mean scores, not a proportion.

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂ is (1.2, 4.8). What can be concluded?
choices: There is convincing evidence that μ₁ is less than μ₂
There is convincing evidence that the two means are equal
There is convincing evidence that μ₁ is greater than μ₂
There is no convincing evidence of a difference
questions.explanation: Every value in the interval is positive, so 0 is not plausible and μ₁ − μ₂ > 0.
choiceExplanations: A positive interval means μ₁ is larger, not smaller.
An interval cannot show that two means are equal, and this one excludes 0.
There is no convincing evidence of a difference only when the interval contains 0.

questions.prompt: Testing H₀: μ = 100, a random sample of 25 gives x̄ = 104 and s = 10. What is the t test statistic?
choiceExplanations: 0.4 divides by s instead of by the standard error s/√n.
This subtracts in the wrong order. Use the statistic minus the null value.
10 divides by s/n = 0.4 instead of by s/√n = 2.

questions.prompt: A random sample of 12 values comes from a population. A dotplot shows strong right skew with two outliers. Is a one-sample t-interval appropriate?
choices: No, because the sample is small and the data show strong skew and outliers
Yes, because n is at least 10
Yes, because the sample was random
No, because the population standard deviation is unknown
questions.explanation: With n = 12 the central limit theorem does not help much, so the normality condition depends on the data. Strong skew and outliers mean t procedures are not reliable here.
choiceExplanations: 10 is not the threshold for means. With n < 30, check the data for strong skew and outliers.
Randomness is required, but the normal condition must also be met.
t procedures are designed for the case where σ is unknown.
